plio-001.title: The sea first floods the Bering land bridge
plio-001.text: Alaska and Siberia were joined by land for a long time. Near the start of the Pliocene, the sea first flooded that land bridge, and marine life could spread between the Arctic and the Pacific. The Bering Strait is thought to have first opened between 7.4 and 4.8 million years ago. The opening did not last unbroken. Afterward the bridge was flooded and restored again and again, as sea level rose and fell, alternately linking the two oceans and the two continents.

plio-003.title: The first tree sloths
plio-003.text: Today's sloths hang from branches, and the first tree sloths appeared around the start of the Pliocene. Their megalonychid cousins show how sizes shifted. Early megalonychids were small and perhaps partly tree-dwelling. By the Pliocene they had grown to about half the size of the later Megalonyx.

plio-005.title: The nimravids die out
plio-005.text: Nimravids, the cat-like carnivores that had led the Oligocene's predators in {{ref:olig-005}}, were still diverse in the Early Miocene. Around the start of the Pliocene they died out, ending a long run as some of the land's top hunters.

plio-009.title: The Zanclean flood refills the Mediterranean
plio-009.text: At its peak, the water pouring through the Strait of Gibraltar may have reached about 100 million cubic metres per second, roughly a thousand times today's Amazon. Atlantic water had broken through and was refilling the dried-out Mediterranean, ending the crisis described in {{ref:mioc-154}}. About ninety percent of the basin may have filled within months to two years. At times, sea level inside rose over 10 metres a day. The sea flooded the deep canyon cut by the ancestral Nile, reaching at least as far as Aswan. The modern Nile then began filling that canyon with sediment. The reconnection marks the start of the Zanclean, the first age of the Pliocene. Not everyone accepts the drama. Sources disagree on whether the Mediterranean refilled in one catastrophic flood or more gradually, and the exact timing remains uncertain.

plio-006.title: The oreodonts vanish
plio-006.text: Oreodonts were plant-eating hoofed mammals that had stayed diverse ever since the Oligocene. In the earliest Pliocene they disappeared, after the turnover described in {{ref:mioc-126}}.

plio-007.title: The Pliocene extinction of big sea animals
plio-007.text: In the Pliocene, 36% of large marine species disappeared. The toll ran unevenly: 55% of marine mammals, 43% of sea turtles, 35% of seabirds and 9% of sharks. Warm-blooded and partly warm-blooded animals were hit harder than cold-blooded ones, which points to a shrinking food supply. Sea level also swung more in the Plio-Pleistocene than at any other time in the Cenozoic, driven by growing polar ice. Those swings damaged coastal habitats and may have helped cause several extinctions. After the Central American Seaway closed, tropical whales declined too.

plio-008.title: The Sierra Nevada lifts and tilts
plio-008.text: Between two and three million years ago, the Sierra Nevada was uplifted and tilted westward. Faulting still lifts it, building steep escarpments on its eastern edge. How old its height is remains disputed. Some read recent river cutting as a sign of young uplift. Others find the northern range little changed since 30-40 million years ago.

plio-004.title: Mount Kenya, a volcano once taller than Kilimanjaro
plio-004.text: Mount Kenya's original summit was probably over 6,000 m high, perhaps 7,000 m, taller than Kilimanjaro is today. This large stratovolcano, a cone built of layered lava and ash, rose on the shoulder of the East African Rift and was active in the Plio-Pleistocene. Since it went extinct, glaciers have worn it down. Its remains are still Africa's second-highest mountain, topped by Batian at 5,199 m.

plio-010.title: The Colorado River starts cutting the Grand Canyon
plio-010.text: The Gulf of California opened 5.3 million years ago and lowered the Colorado River's base level, the low point it drains toward. Erosion sped up, and most of the canyon's depth was cut by 1.2 Ma. Several studies hold that the river set its course 5-6 million years ago. The canyon's age is debated, though: other studies put parts at 17 to 70 million years old, and segments probably formed at different times.

plio-011.title: The great white shark appears
plio-011.text: The great white shark evolved about 5.3 million years ago. Its young had safe places to grow. Abundant juvenile teeth along Chile's Coquimbo Region show that Pliocene coasts there served as great white shark nurseries. Its rise later gained from the decline of a bigger rival, told in {{ref:plio-037}}.

plio-012.title: The Pliocene Warm Interval
plio-012.text: Carbon dioxide levels in the Pliocene were similar to today's. That makes this time a favorite natural experiment: the interval is often treated as a preview of near-future warming. From about 5.3 to 2.7 Ma, the Pliocene Warm Interval interrupted the long-term cooling trend. The epoch opened warmer than the cool Messinian before it. Ice sheets were unstable. Their collapses were much more common in the early to mid Pliocene, between 5 and 3 Ma. The oceans stayed relatively warm, though they kept slowly cooling. The warmest stretch is told in {{ref:plio-045}}.

plio-013.title: Bluff Downs, a Pliocene Queensland riverland
plio-013.text: Between about 5.2 and 3.6 million years ago, animals died and were buried beside large water bodies fringed by riverside forest at Bluff Downs, northern Queensland. It is one of Australia's most significant Pliocene sites, with marsupials from both living and extinct families. A basalt flow dated 3.62 Ma caps the fossil beds, which are at least 4 million years old.

plio-014.title: Kauaʻi rises over the Hawaiian hotspot
plio-014.text: Kauaʻi, the oldest of the main Hawaiian islands, is 5.1 ± 0.2 million years old. It formed as the Pacific Plate passed over the Hawaiʻi hotspot, a fixed source of rising magma. The plate keeps moving west-northwest, carrying each volcano away, so the chain gets younger toward the southeast.

plio-015.title: The Colorado Plateau and River take their modern shape
plio-015.text: About 5 million years ago the Colorado Plateau reached its present height, and the Colorado River settled into a course close to today's. Plateau uplift and the opening of the Gulf of California rearranged the river and its tributaries. About 4 million years ago, the Colorado began reaching the Salton Trough, then still connected to the Gulf.

plio-016.title: The last giant-toothed sperm whales
plio-016.text: Teeth from Australia and South Africa show that Livyatan or a close relative still hunted around 5 million years ago, possibly worldwide. By the early Pliocene these giant-toothed sperm whales were gone. Cooling probably made baleen whales larger and fewer, and the predators that fed on them declined with them.

plio-017.title: Thylacoleo, the marsupial lion
plio-017.text: Thylacoleo, the marsupial lion, first appeared in the Pliocene. Its early species, T. crassidentatus, about 5 million years ago, was the size of a large dog. Later species grew to the weight of a lioness. The genus became Australia's apex predator, the only one of its family until the end of the Pleistocene.

plio-018.title: The Paratethys breaks into inland seas
plio-018.text: The Black, Caspian and Aral seas are the remnants of the Paratethys. From about 5 million years ago the old sea grew steadily shallower and largely dried out. During the Pliocene it split into a few inland seas, at times fully cut off from each other. The Pliocene Caspian was a small lake with no outlet.

plio-019.title: A Pliocene burst of ignimbrites in the Puna
plio-019.text: Between 5 and 3.8 Ma, huge ignimbrite eruptions struck the front of the volcanic arc in the northern Puna, part of a magma pulse around 4 Ma. The Puripicar ignimbrite, about 4.2 Ma, alone held some 1,500 cubic kilometres. Later giants followed: the Tara ignimbrite at 3.49 Ma (800 km3) and Pastos Grandes at 2.89 Ma (1,500 km3).

plio-020.title: The Gray Fossil Site, a Tennessee sinkhole
plio-020.text: Between 4.9 and 4.5 million years ago, a sinkhole pond in a warm, wet Tennessee forest trapped plants and animals. It is the first site of its age known from Appalachia, with new species of red panda, rhinoceros, pond turtle and hickory. Its fossils show eastern North America still shared a living link with Eurasia then.

plio-022.title: The Kilgore Tuff supereruption
plio-022.text: The Kilgore Tuff eruption in eastern Idaho, rated VEI 8, blasted out about 1,800 cubic kilometres of ash and left a caldera 80 by 60 km. It was the last caldera-forming eruption of the Heise field, active for over 2 million years above the Yellowstone hotspot. As the hotspot track moved northeast, the Picabo and Heise centres subsided.

plio-023.title: Ardi, a skeleton caught between trees and ground
plio-023.text: Ardi is a 4.4-million-year-old female skeleton, the most complete specimen of the early hominin Ardipithecus ramidus. Her species lived in the Afar region of Ethiopia about 4.4 million years ago. Her body shows two worlds at once. Ardi's pelvis shows that walking on two legs was well under way, yet her hands and limbs could still climb trees. Fossils of at least nine more individuals from As Duma in the Afar date to 4.51-4.32 million years ago. The older A. kadabba, met in {{ref:mioc-156}}, is considered its direct ancestor.

plio-024.title: Australopithecus anamensis, the first australopith
plio-024.text: The oldest known species of Australopithecus, A. anamensis, lived roughly 4.3 to 3.8 million years ago. Its first fossils came from Kanapoi and Allia Bay in northern Kenya, and the Allia Bay finds give the earliest evidence of a two-legged gait. The genus probably arose in eastern Africa around 4 Ma. It later spread across the continent and died out somewhat after 2 Ma. A nearly complete 3.8-million-year-old skull from Ethiopia shows that A. anamensis overlapped in time with its successor, A. afarensis, in {{ref:plio-027}}.

plio-025.title: La Pacana's Atana supereruption
plio-025.text: At 2,500-3,500 cubic kilometres, the Atana ignimbrite is the fifth-largest explosive eruption known. It came from La Pacana caldera in the Chilean Andes between about 4.2 and 3.8 million years ago. A much smaller sister eruption, the Toconao ignimbrite, came out at almost the same time. The rocks show no sign of a pause between the two, as if one long event had produced both.

plio-026.title: The Hagerman Fossil Beds and their horse
plio-026.text: The Hagerman fossil beds in Idaho span at least 4 million to 3.07 million years ago and hold at least 200 species. They are among the richest deposits of North America's Blancan age. They also hold the largest known concentration of the Hagerman horse, Equus simplicidens.

plio-028.title: Glyptodon, the armored giant
plio-028.text: Glyptodon was an armadillo relative with a shell of hundreds of bony plates, 2 m long and 400 kg. It and its cousin Glyptotherium evolved in South America from about 3.9 million years ago. This plant-eater lasted from about 3.2 million years ago until about 11,000 years ago, into the early Holocene.

plio-027.title: Australopithecus afarensis walks East Africa
plio-027.text: Selam was a three-year-old girl who died at Dikika, Ethiopia, 3.3 million years ago, about 100,000 years before Lucy. She belonged to Australopithecus afarensis, which lived in East Africa from about 3.9 to 2.9 million years ago. The 3.58-million-year-old Kadanuumuu skeleton suggests the species already walked fully upright by 3.6 Ma, though not all researchers agree. Tooth chemistry shows a flexible diet, from forest plants to savanna plants. Life was dangerous. Africa then held more large carnivores than today, including hyenas and saber-toothed cats, which likely preyed on australopithecines.

plio-029.title: A green North Africa
plio-029.text: North Africa was once green. From about 3.8 to 3.3 million years ago, it went through an extended humid period. Tropical forests in the northwest reached as far as Cape Blanc until around 3.5 Ma. A significant river flowed across the Sahara until 3.35 Ma. Then the trade winds began to dominate, and the region started down the road to desert.

plio-030.title: The woolly rhino's ancestor lives in Tibet
plio-030.text: The woolly rhinoceros's lineage began high on the Tibetan Plateau. Coelodonta thibetana, the oldest known species of its genus, lived there about 3.7 million years ago. The genus later spread to Siberia, Mongolia and China. The woolly rhinoceros itself appeared later, in the Middle Pleistocene.

plio-031.title: Footprints in the ash at Laetoli
plio-031.text: About 3.7 million years ago, three hominins walked across fresh volcanic ash at Laetoli in Tanzania, one stepping in the prints of another. Soft rain then cemented the powdery ash into tuff, rock made of compacted volcanic ash, sealing the tracks. Their makers were probably Australopithecus. The prints closely resemble modern human footprints. They were then the oldest known evidence of hominin bipedalism. Together with leg bones, the trackways suggest A. afarensis walked well on two legs, though less efficiently than humans.

plio-032.title: Little Foot, the most complete early hominin
plio-032.text: Little Foot is about 90% complete, the most complete early hominin skeleton known. It comes from the Sterkfontein caves of South Africa. A 2015 date of 3.67 million years would make it the earliest known South African australopith. That date is controversial, with estimates from 2.2 to 3.67 million years, and its species is also disputed.

plio-034.title: Megatherium, the elephant-sized sloth
plio-034.text: Megatherium was a giant ground sloth of South America, and its best-known species, M. americanum, reached 3.5-4 tonnes, the size of an elephant. Its oldest remains come from Bolivia and the Pampas and are at least 3.6 million years old. The genus lasted to the end of the Late Pleistocene.

plio-035.title: El'gygytgyn, an impact lake that records Arctic climate
plio-035.text: About 3.6 million years ago, an impact on Siberia's Chukchi Peninsula blasted out a crater 18 km across. The crater now holds a lake about 12 km wide. Its sediments are a climate archive, showing mid-Pliocene Arctic summers 8 °C warmer than today.

plio-037.title: Megalodon disappears
plio-037.text: Megalodon, a shark estimated at 14-24 m long, was among the most powerful predators ever. It hunted worldwide from about 23 million years ago, as {{ref:mioc-027}} describes. A 2019 statistical reanalysis of its fossils moved its extinction back to about 3.6 million years ago, earlier than the long-assumed 2.6 million years. Several pressures probably combined. The seas cooled, and falling sea levels shrank its warm nursery waters. Small baleen whales, its prey, declined. Early killer whales were once blamed, but that now looks unlikely; rivalry with white sharks may have played a part. Its loss let great white sharks spread into its waters, and baleen whales grew markedly larger afterward.

plio-036.title: Mammoths and Asian elephants leave Africa
plio-036.text: Around 3.6 to 3.2 million years ago, the elephant genera Elephas and Mammuthus, the mammoths, migrated out of Africa. Mammoths took the route through the Sinai Peninsula. By 3.2 million years ago they had spread into Eurasia, reaching Europe around 3 million years ago. In Asia, elephants, gomphotheres and stegodonts thrived, though proboscidean diversity fell sharply during the Late Pliocene. Back in Africa, mammoths became confined to the north of the continent.

plio-038.title: Australopiths reach Central Africa
plio-038.text: Jaw fossils from Koro Toro in Chad, about 3.5 million years old, are the first and only australopiths known from Central Africa. They show australopiths ranged widely, not just in the east and south. These hominins lived in lakeside grassland by an expanded 'Lake Mega-Chad', eating mostly savanna foods. Many researchers assign them to A. afarensis.

plio-039.title: Kenyanthropus, a flat-faced rival
plio-039.text: Kenyanthropus was a flat-faced, small-toothed hominin from Lake Turkana in Kenya. Its type skull is about 3.5 million years old, and its fossils span about 3.5 to 3.2 Ma. It shows that more than one hominin lineage lived alongside A. afarensis. It lived among forest and grassland, and may have made the Lomekwian stone tools found nearby.

plio-040.title: Camels in the High Arctic
plio-040.text: Camels once lived inside the Arctic Circle. Fragmentary remains referred to Paracamelus, about 3.4 million years old, come from Ellesmere Island. The world was then 2-3 °C warmer than today, and the island was covered in boreal forest. Collagen sequences confirm these Arctic camels were close relatives of modern Camelus.

plio-041.title: Dikika's disputed cut marks
plio-041.text: At Dikika in Ethiopia, a rib and a thigh bone from hoofed animals bear cut marks, the rib also some crushing. If stone tools made them, they would be the oldest evidence of butchering with sharp-edged tools, at 3.4 million years. The claim is disputed. The bones lay in sandstone, where abrasive sand and gravel also scratched them.

plio-044.title: Lomekwi: the oldest stone tools
plio-044.text: In West Turkana, Kenya, 3.3 million years ago, someone struck one stone against another. The flakes they left at Lomekwi 3 are the oldest known stone tools. The method was simple. The toolmaker pounded a core on an anvil or hit it with a hammerstone, using volcanic rock gathered within 100 m. Who made them is unknown. Kenyanthropus platyops, a 3.5-3.2-million-year-old hominin from Lake Turkana met in {{ref:plio-039}}, may have been the earliest tool user. There are hints of something older. Cut-marked bones about 3.4 million years old from Ethiopia's Lower Awash Valley may be indirect evidence of tool use, though that claim is weaker. These tools open a long chapter. The Paleolithic, which covers almost all of humanity's prehistoric technology, begins with the first stone tools about 3.3 million years ago.

plio-046.title: The Phoenix plate stops sinking
plio-046.text: For over 100 million years, the Phoenix plate had been sinking beneath its neighbors. About 3.3 million years ago, spreading on the Antarctic-Phoenix Ridge stopped, and its subduction slowed or ceased. The plate's remnant was absorbed into the Antarctic plate.

plio-047.title: A possible impact in Argentina
plio-047.text: Around 3.3 million years ago, at the start of the Marplatan land-mammal age, a cosmic impact may have struck Argentina. It has been suggested as a cause of a turnover in South American animals. Both the impact and that link remain uncertain, and the sources call the idea controversial.

plio-045.title: The Mid-Piacenzian Warm Period
plio-045.text: Between 3.3 and 3.0 million years ago, carbon dioxide stood near 400 ppm, the level of the year 2000. Global temperatures ran 2-3 °C above today's. This peak of Pliocene warmth is also called the Pliocene Thermal Maximum. The poles warmed most. Arctic summers were about 8 °C warmer than now, and models suggest the Arctic above 70°N was 10-20 °C warmer, with little change in the tropics. Greenland's ice shrank to its highest eastern and southern peaks. Global sea level stood about 25 m higher than today. In southeastern European lakes, viviparid snails diversified rapidly as temperatures rose by as much as 10 °C between 3.3 and 2.9 Ma.

openers.pliocene-epoch: The Pliocene opened with a flood. Atlantic water broke through at the Strait of Gibraltar and refilled the dried-out Mediterranean. Soon the sea first flooded the land bridge between Alaska and Siberia too. From about 5.3 to 2.7 million years ago, a warm interval interrupted the long-term cooling trend. Old groups such as the oreodonts and the cat-like nimravids died out, the great white shark evolved, and a marine extinction wiped out 36% of large marine species.
